title: 2D Asset generation pipeline
author: Calm-Chip-8039
selftext:
I am having trouble finding a workflow with claude to where it can generate 2d assets.  It seems like 3d is covered, but im struggling with 2d.

For instance im making a tank game. And I want like 50 different skins.  How do you do that?

Any help suggestions or ideas are appreciated.

replies.author: dilberry
replies.body: You can just give your dot a reference image, or ask it to make one, and then ask for the sprite sheet. It will give you a big sheet of movements, perspectives, etc to animate or integrate. That's all there is to it... I have a fancy app I made to try to do the same thing, but ChatGPT is so much better at it. You'll get a full sheet of content in 2-3 minutes and it's damn good at it.

comments.author: zayelion
comments.body: I use comfyui. I have Astra make a json payload of prompts; it feeds them into comfy via API and then I just wait. Then I pick the best of them and refine them with Astra's imagegen. Then I put them back in to get standardized by the game code and then save the visual result for reuse to save on rendering while the game is active. (it also strips the prompts out)

comments.author: macuseri686
comments.body:
So the main issue with using a standard AI tool like Claude for 2d assets like spritesheet animations is that those models can't output transparency, and even state of the art image generation models like Chat GPT image gen and Google nano banana have no concept of subject alignment, consistent movement speed, and alignment between frames. You'll spend more time cleaning up the output than you saved generating it. [https://gamelabstudio.co/blog/why-ai-cant-make-game-ready-spritesheets](https://gamelabstudio.co/blog/why-ai-cant-make-game-ready-spritesheets) . 

https://i.redd.it/88z53qan67th1.gif

I actually built [Gamelabs Studio](https://gamelabstudio.co/ai-sprite-sheet-generator?ref=reddit.com) to solve these problems for a steampunk tower defence game i released last year. It handles transparent spritesheets, consistent angles/palette across frames, and tileable textures. It also has an MCP that you can use directly inside your coding agent

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: Vertex painting. Or you paint the tank and manually unwrap the UVs in a way that every piece is clearly identifiable for what it is (barrel, chassis, tires, etc) rather than to conserve texture space which can lead to very chaotic UVs, then you can give the texture to Image 2.5 and it will probably be able to generate skins from it. Then for PBR you'd have to find an AI (there are several) that can make accurate PBR textures from the diffuse.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Google or AI can explain it better. It's basically just assigning materials to faces of the model in vertex/region groups. So I can select my entire tank barrel and paint it a material called 'tank\_barrel\_mat', then do the same for wheels, the same for the main metal body, the same for various attachments. Then you go and tell your agent to come up with a bunch of material schemes you can swap between for all of those groups. Depending on how fancy you want to get with materials, you may want to have it utilize gradients, textures, or various shader nodes (depending on your engine) to go crazy. You can provide it refs if you have something specific in mind. Either way it can then go and create sets of materials that can be utilized interchangeably for each of those parts. So you might have some kind of red/black  striped chassis material, and swap out you tank barrel for chrome, or gold, silver, rusted metal, whatever. You can also have your agent utilize freely available materials as inspirations for the material nodes in whatever engine you're using (not sure if every engine uses node graphs, but... they're fairly common for their shader/material systems), and that might help improve the results.

Anyway, when your UVs / poly placement in models makes sense, it's superior in many ways to texturing something, as long as you're not looking for very fine details that are difficult to do programmatically (like a mole/blemish on one side of a face.) Though depending on the complexity of the final materials it may be best to rasterize them into textures anyway because the computations can actually be more demanding than loading even a mid-large sized static texture. Depends on where your performance bottlenecks are though. If you did rasterize, then you'd be doing texture swaps rather than material swaps in game.
